title: The First Five Minutes — Scene Size-Up & Primary Assessment
transcript:
"You pull up to a call at 2 a.m. Dispatch said 'difficulty breathing.' That's all you've got. The next five minutes will determine everything that happens after — and most of it has nothing to do with the ambulance."

Welcome back to the podcast. Today we're talking about the first five minutes of every call: scene size-up and the primary assessment. This is the foundation everything else sits on.

Before you touch a patient, you answer three questions. Is the scene safe? What's the mechanism of injury or nature of illness? How many patients do I have, and do I need more resources?

Scene safety isn't a checkbox — it's continuous. Traffic, bystanders, weapons, hazards, pets, weather. If the scene isn't safe, you don't enter. Period.

General impression, level of consciousness, airway, breathing, circulation. Find and fix life threats before you move on. If the airway is compromised, nothing else matters yet.

The most common mistake is skipping the primary assessment to "get vitals." Vitals are data. The primary assessment is a decision. Don't let the monitor replace your eyes and hands.

Next episode: secondary assessment and history-taking. Until then — scene safe, ABCs first, and drive safe.

title: Airway: The One Skill You Can't Fake
transcript:
"Every EMT skill can be fumbled and recovered — except the airway. You get one shot to get this right, and the patient's brain starts counting down in minutes."

Today: airway management for the EMT. Positioning, suctioning, airway adjuncts, and knowing when to escalate.

Head-tilt chin-lift for medical patients without suspected spinal injury. Jaw-thrust when you suspect trauma. Simple, but position matters more than people think.

Blood, vomit, secretions — suction early. Don't suction longer than 10–15 seconds at a time, and pre-oxygenate when you can.

OPA for patients without a gag reflex; NPA when they have one. Size matters — measure from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe for an OPA, nostril to earlobe for an NPA.

If you can't maintain the airway with basic skills, that's an ALS intercept or rapid transport decision. Know your protocol.

Airway first, always. Next week: breathing and ventilation. Stay sharp.

title: CPR That Actually Works — High-Quality BLS
transcript:
"The difference between 10% and 40% survival from cardiac arrest isn't the drug — it's the compression. Depth, rate, recoil, and interruptions."

Today we're breaking down high-quality CPR — the science and the street-level execution.

100–120 compressions per minute. At least 2 inches deep in adults. Full recoil. Minimize interruptions to under 10 seconds.

Rotate compressors every 2 minutes. Communicate in closed loops: "You — compressions. You — airway. You — monitor." Silence kills.

Leaning on the chest, shallow compressions, long pauses for rhythm checks, and forgetting to switch compressors before fatigue sets in.

High-quality CPR is a team sport with a metronome. Practice it until it's automatic.

Compress hard, fast, and let it recoil. See you next episode.

title: Trauma Triage — Mechanism of Injury & Transport Decisions
transcript:
"Not every trauma patient looks sick — and some look fine until they don't. Mechanism of injury is your early warning system."

Today: reading mechanism of injury and making transport decisions in trauma.

Energy transfer tells the story. Falls, MVCs, penetrating trauma, blunt force. Ask: what forces acted on this body, and where?

Altered mental status, hypotension, tachycardia, unequal pupils, distended abdomen, pelvic instability, long bone deformity. These change your destination and your urgency.

Trauma center vs. local ED. Time vs. capability. Know your regional protocol and when to request ALS or air medical.

Spinal motion restriction when indicated — not automatically. Splint, secure, and go. Scene time is a vital sign.

Read the mechanism, respect the red flags, and don't linger. Next: medical emergencies.

title: The Medical Call That Looks Like a Trauma — Altered Mental Status
transcript:
"AMS is a symptom, not a diagnosis. And the cause might be in their pocket, their glucose meter, or their medication list."

Today: the differential for altered mental status and how to work it up systematically.

AEIOU-TIPS: Alcohol, Epilepsy, Insulin, Opiates, Uremia, Trauma, Infection, Psych, Stroke. Walk through each.

Glucose first. Oxygen and ventilation. Pupils, posture, and purposeful movement. Look for medical alert jewelry and medication lists.

Time last known well. Facial droop, arm drift, speech. Note the time and transport to a stroke-capable facility.

Agitation can be hypoxia, hypoglycemia, or head injury. Rule out reversible causes before assuming behavioral.

Find the cause, not just the symptom. Next episode: patient communication.

title: Talking to Patients Who Don't Want to Talk
transcript:
"You can be technically perfect and still lose the patient — because trust is a clinical skill."

Today: communication on the street. De-escalation, consent, and the art of the difficult conversation.

Introduce yourself, explain what you're doing, and ask permission when you can. Narrate your care.

Lower your voice, slow your pace, give space, and avoid power struggles. Validate before you correct.

Capacity, informed consent, documentation. If they refuse, make sure it's informed and documented — and know your protocol for when to escalate.

Plain language, no jargon, and let silence do some work. You don't have to fix the emotion — just be present.

Communication is a skill you practice, not a personality trait. Next: documentation.

title: Documentation That Protects You
transcript:
"If it isn't written down, it didn't happen — and in EMS, that's a legal statement, not a cliché."

Today: writing a patient care report that's accurate, defensible, and actually useful.

Subjective, objective, assessment, plan. Keep it chronological and specific.

Quote the patient. Describe what you saw, not what you concluded. "Patient stated 'I can't breathe'" beats "patient was in distress."

Document capacity, risks explained, and who was present. Time-stamp everything.

Write it as if a lawyer and a paramedic will both read it — because they might.

Document like your license depends on it. Because it does. Thanks for listening.

title: Burnout, Sleep, and the Long Shift
transcript:
"You can't pour from an empty cup — and in EMS, the cup gets emptied at 3 a.m. on a 24-hour shift."

Today: provider wellness. Sleep, stress, and staying in the job you love.

Sleep debt is cumulative. Nap strategically, protect your off-duty sleep, and don't normalize chronic exhaustion.

Debrief after critical calls. Talk to someone. Know your EAP and peer support resources.

Say no when you can. Take your breaks. Off-duty means off-duty.

Warning signs: cynicism, isolation, substance use, intrusive thoughts. Getting help is a professional skill.

Take care of the caregiver. See you next time — and get some sleep.
